newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-Kohl praises U.S. on jobs as Bonn under fire.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Kohl praises U.S. on jobs as Bonn under fire.

text.p: Chancellor Helmut Kohl, facing a barrage of criticism over his country's crippling jobless rates, said on Sunday Germans should follow the American example and adopt a more flexible approach to work.

At home, unions, politicians and economists clashed over whether sluggish growth, the absence of structural reform, or the length of the working week was to blame for Germany's jobs crisis, while Kohl, meeting group of seven (G7) leaders in Denver, praised the U.S. for its flexible labour markets.

"We can learn a lot from the Americans in the way that they have developed a more dynamic situation. They are more flexible, more spontaneous and more mobile," Kohl said in an interview with Germany's ZDF television.

But Kohl also cast doubt on whether Germany would be able to follow the U.S.'s path. "This thinking is simply impossible in Germany," he told ZDF's Bonn Direkt programme, according to a transcript of the interview released in Bonn.
Latest figures show that 4.26 million people are out of work in Germany, 11.1 percent of the workforce. In the U.S., unemployment is running at 4.8 percent.

Klaus Zwickel, chairman of IG Metall, Germany's largest trade union, told a weekend meeting in Hannover that Kohl's government had failed to fullfil its promises and called on it to admit defeat and step down.
"It is high time for this government to step down," Zwickel said, adding that Germans were fed up with trusting in higher corporate turnover and "exploding" profits to cut unemployment.

Retaliating against what he termed Zwickel's "one-sided, party political propaganda", Peter Hintze, general secretary of Kohl's Christian Democrats (CDU), said the union leader's policy of reducing working hours had led only to rising labour costs and the destruction of jobs.
"We need an investment-friendly climate which will create new jobs," Hintze said. "Greater flexibility and a reduction in labour costs are needed for that."
He said the IG Metall chief should abstain from such "crass polemics" and concentrate instead on cooperation to secure Germany's position.

But Horst Siebert, a leading German economist and a member of the government's "five wise men" economic advisory council, said the country must undergo far-reaching reform of the social welfare system to ease unemployment levels.

Lashing out at the stability and jobs pact agreed by European leaders in Amsterdam, Siebert said such agreements were of litle use in the fight against joblessness, since its causes were different in every country.

Germany's labour markets were suffering above all under the burden of high wage levels and structual problems, and relying on an expected pick-up in growth rates was not enough. "Growth alone cannot eliminate Germany's jobs crisis," he told the Welt am Sonntag newspaper.
Criticism of the EU Amsterdam deal was also levelled by Heide Simonis, state premier for Schleswig Holstein and a member the opposition Social Democats (SPD).
"(The pact) is nothing but empty phrases. It was formulated very vaguely so that no-one would lose face," he told the weekly Spiegel magazine Germany.
Simonis said Germany should introduce job-sharing initiatives, cut working hours and wages accordingly, and consider a reduction in the minimum starting wage for the long-term unemployed.
